\section[\gu{બોલવું}]{\gu{બોલવું} (bolvũ) — \textquotedblleft{}to speak,\textquotedblright{} your first full verb}

\label{lesson:GU-C05-bolvun}



\begin{quote}
So far, \textquotedblleft{}to be.\textquotedblright{} Here is a verb that \emph{does} something — in a shape you'll see on every Gujarati verb.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{બો}} (\emph{bo}) + \textbf{\gu{લ}} (\emph{la}) + \textbf{\gu{વું}} (\emph{vũ}, with the nasal) $\to$ \textbf{\gu{બોલવું}} (\emph{bolvũ}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{બોલવું}} (\emph{bolvũ}, \textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{}) is a native Indo-Aryan verb (the same \emph{bol-} as Hindi \emph{bolnā} and Punjabi \emph{bolṇā}). Its ending \textbf{-\gu{વું}} (\emph{-vũ}) is Gujarati's infinitive marker — the \textquotedblleft{}to \_\_\_\textquotedblright{} form: \emph{bol-vũ} \textquotedblleft{}to speak,\textquotedblright{} \emph{maḷ-vũ} \textquotedblleft{}to meet\textquotedblright{} (from \emph{maḷīshũ}), \emph{āv-vũ} \textquotedblleft{}to come\textquotedblright{} (behind \emph{āvjo}). Strip the \emph{-vũ} and you have the \textbf{stem} (\emph{bol-}).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: stem + person + copula}]
To say \textquotedblleft{}I speak,\textquotedblright{} Gujarati adds a person-ending to the stem and follows it with the copula:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hũ bolũ chhũ} — I speak
  \item \emph{tũ bole chhe} — you speak (familiar)
  \item \emph{tame bolo chho} — you speak (respectful)
  \item \emph{te bole chhe} — he/she speaks
\end{itemize}

The simple present is the same for a man or a woman — Gujarati saves its \textbf{three genders} for adjectives and the past tense, not the plain present.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bolvũ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the infinitive ending every Gujarati verb takes (\emph{-vũ})
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I speak\textquotedblright{} — \emph{hũ bolũ chhũ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What ending marks a Gujarati infinitive, and how do you say \textquotedblleft{}I speak\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{-vũ}; \emph{hũ bolũ chhũ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{હું} \gu{ગુજરાતી} \gu{બોલું} \gu{છું}]{\gu{હું} \gu{ગુજરાતી} \gu{બોલું} \gu{છું} (hũ gujarātī bolũ chhũ) — \textquotedblleft{}I speak Gujarati\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GU-C05-hun-gujarati-bolun-chhun}



\begin{quote}
Your first complete, moving sentence — and the language names itself after a people who arrived on horseback.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{ગુજરાતી}} (\emph{gujarātī}): \textbf{\gu{ગુ}} (\emph{gu}) + \textbf{\gu{જ}} (\emph{ja}) + \textbf{\gu{રા}} (\emph{rā}) + \textbf{\gu{તી}} (\emph{tī}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{હું} \gu{ગુજરાતી} \gu{બોલું} \gu{છું}} = \textbf{\gu{હું}} (\emph{hũ}, \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\gu{ગુજરાતી}} (\emph{gujarātī}, the object) + \textbf{\gu{બોલું} \gu{છું}} (\emph{bolũ chhũ}, \textquotedblleft{}speak\textquotedblright{}) — \textquotedblleft{}I Gujarati speak,\textquotedblright{} verb last. The name \textbf{\gu{ગુજરાત}} (\emph{Gujarāt}) comes from the \textbf{Gurjar} — a people who entered western India around the 6th–8th centuries and gave their name to the land (\emph{Gurjara-deśa} $\to$ \emph{Gujarāt}); \emph{gujarātī} is \textquotedblleft{}{[}the language{]} of Gujarat.\textquotedblright{} So the language is named after a people, and the region after them in turn.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: no gender in the plain present}]
\emph{Bolũ chhũ} is the same whether a man or a woman says it — Gujarati's \textbf{three genders} live in its adjectives (\emph{sāro/sārī/sārũ}) and its past tense, but the simple present \textquotedblleft{}I speak\textquotedblright{} is gender-free. And because \emph{chhũ} already carries \textquotedblleft{}I,\textquotedblright{} you could drop \emph{hũ}: \emph{gujarātī bolũ chhũ}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hũ gujarātī bolũ chhũ\textquotedblright{}
  \item what \emph{Gujarāt} is named after (the \emph{Gurjar} people)
  \item does \textquotedblleft{}I speak\textquotedblright{} change for a man vs. a woman? (No — not in the plain present)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I speak Gujarati,\textquotedblright{} and give the origin of the name. (\emph{Hũ gujarātī bolũ chhũ}; from the \emph{Gurjar} people, who named the land Gujarat.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{કામ} \gu{કરવું}]{\gu{કામ} \gu{કરવું} (kām karvũ) — \textquotedblleft{}to work\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GU-C05-kaam-karvun}



\begin{quote}
The last verb of the chapter — from the single most productive root in the whole family, one you have met before.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{કામ}} (\emph{kām}, \textquotedblleft{}work\textquotedblright{}): \textbf{\gu{કા}} (\emph{kā}) + \textbf{\gu{મ}} (\emph{ma}). \textbf{\gu{કરવું}} (\emph{karvũ}, \textquotedblleft{}to do\textquotedblright{}): \textbf{\gu{ક}} (\emph{ka}) + \textbf{\gu{ર}} (\emph{ra}) + \textbf{\gu{વું}} (\emph{vũ}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{કરવું}} (\emph{karvũ}, \textquotedblleft{}to do, to make\textquotedblright{}) is from Sanskrit \textbf{√\gu{કૃ}} (\emph{√kṛ}, \textquotedblleft{}to do\textquotedblright{}), from PIE \textbf{*k\textsuperscript{w}er-} — one of Sanskrit's most productive roots, met in \emph{namaskār} (\textquotedblleft{}the \textbf{making} of a bow\textquotedblright{}) and \emph{karma} (\textquotedblleft{}a thing \textbf{done}\textquotedblright{}). And \textbf{\gu{કામ}} (\emph{kām}, \textquotedblleft{}work\textquotedblright{}) is itself from Sanskrit \emph{karma} — so \textquotedblleft{}work-do\textquotedblright{} is, at root, \textquotedblleft{}\emph{kṛ}-thing \emph{kṛ}-do.\textquotedblright{} Like Hindi, Gujarati builds compound verbs as \textbf{noun + \gu{કરવું}}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\gu{કામ} \gu{કરવું}} (\emph{kām karvũ}) = \textquotedblleft{}work-do\textquotedblright{} = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to work}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{\gu{વાત} \gu{કરવી}} (\emph{vāt karvī}) = \textquotedblleft{}to converse\textquotedblright{} (\emph{vāt}, \textquotedblleft{}talk\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

So \emph{hũ kām karũ chhũ} = \textquotedblleft{}I work.\textquotedblright{} Learn \emph{karvũ} and a whole grammar of \textquotedblleft{}do-verbs\textquotedblright{} opens up — the same one behind Hindi's \emph{kām karnā} and Bengali's \emph{kāj karā}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kām karvũ\textquotedblright{} (to work)
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I work\textquotedblright{} — \emph{hũ kām karũ chhũ}
  \item the Chapter-1 word that shares its root (\emph{namaskār}-style — actually \emph{ābhār}? no; recall \emph{karma}, from \emph{kṛ})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Sanskrit root is \emph{karvũ} from, and what is \emph{kām} (\textquotedblleft{}work\textquotedblright{}) from? (\emph{√kṛ}, \textquotedblleft{}to do\textquotedblright{}; \emph{kām} $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{karma} — both from \emph{kṛ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{રહેવું}]{\gu{રહેવું} (rahevũ) — \textquotedblleft{}to live, to stay\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GU-C05-rahevun}



\begin{quote}
A second verb, so you can say where you live.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{ર}} (\emph{ra}) + \textbf{\gu{હે}} (\emph{he}) + \textbf{\gu{વું}} (\emph{vũ}) $\to$ \textbf{\gu{રહેવું}} (\emph{rahevũ}). The familiar \emph{-vũ} infinitive.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{રહેવું}} (\emph{rahevũ}, \textquotedblleft{}to live, to remain, to stay\textquotedblright{}) is from Sanskrit \textbf{\gu{રહ્}} (\emph{rah-}, \textquotedblleft{}to remain\textquotedblright{}) — the same root as Hindi \emph{rahnā} and Punjabi \emph{rahiṇā}. \textquotedblleft{}I live in Ahmedabad\textquotedblright{} is \textbf{\gu{હું} \gu{અમદાવાદમાં} \gu{રહું} \gu{છું}} (\emph{hũ Amdāvādmā rahũ chhũ}) — stem \emph{rah-} + person + copula, exactly like \emph{bolvũ}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} comes after the noun}]
\textbf{\gu{અમદાવાદમાં}} (\emph{Amdāvādmā}) = \emph{Ahmedabad} + \textbf{-\gu{માં}} (\emph{-mā}, \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{}), glued to the \textbf{end} of the noun. Gujarati, like Hindi, uses \textbf{post}positions where English uses prepositions: \textquotedblleft{}Ahmedabad-in I live,\textquotedblright{} the verb last.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}rahevũ\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I live in Ahmedabad\textquotedblright{} — \emph{hũ Amdāvādmā rahũ chhũ}
  \item where \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} (\emph{-mā}) sits — glued to the end of the noun
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What root is \emph{rahevũ} from, and where does \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} go? (Sanskrit \emph{rah-} \textquotedblleft{}to remain\textquotedblright{}; \emph{-mā} \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} attaches to the \textbf{end} of the noun.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 7 — The first verbs}

\label{lesson:GU-C05-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Three verbs, one engine — build real sentences about yourself.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{How to answer — build the sentences}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I speak Gujarati\textquotedblright{} — \emph{hũ gujarātī bolũ chhũ}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I live in Ahmedabad\textquotedblright{} — \emph{hũ Amdāvādmā rahũ chhũ}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I work\textquotedblright{} — \emph{hũ kām karũ chhũ}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}you (resp.) speak Gujarati\textquotedblright{} — \emph{tame gujarātī bolo chho}
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens — the engine}]
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the ending every infinitive carries (\emph{-vũ})
  \item the shape of the present (stem + person + the copula \emph{chhũ/chhe/chho})
  \item where the verb sits, and where \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} sits (verb last; \emph{-mā} after the noun)
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — roots you now carry}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bolvũ} \textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{} (native; \emph{bol-}, like Hindi/Punjabi)
  \item \emph{rahevũ} \textquotedblleft{}to live\textquotedblright{} $\leftarrow$ \emph{rah-} \textquotedblleft{}to remain\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{karvũ} \textquotedblleft{}to do\textquotedblright{} $\leftarrow$ \emph{√kṛ}; \emph{kām} \textquotedblleft{}work\textquotedblright{} $\leftarrow$ \emph{karma} (both from \emph{kṛ})
  \item \emph{gujarātī} $\leftarrow$ the \emph{Gurjar} people, who named the land Gujarat
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
In one breath, tell me your language, your city, and your work in Gujarati. (\emph{Hũ gujarātī bolũ chhũ. Hũ … rahũ chhũ. Hũ kām karũ chhũ.})
\end{tcolorbox}
